passages.t: The army at war, and the king at home
passages.happening:
‘In the spring, at the time when kings march out to war, David sent out Joab and his servants with the whole army of Israel. They destroyed the Ammonites and besieged Rabbah, but David remained in Jerusalem’ (verse 1).

One evening David gets up from his bed and walks on the palace roof, and from the roof he sees a woman bathing. He sends to ask about her, and he is told, “This is Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam and the wife of Uriah the Hittite” (verse 3).

“Then David sent messengers to get her, and when she came to him, he slept with her” (verse 4). The narrator adds that she had just purified herself from her uncleanness, and she goes home. She conceives, and she sends David word: “I am pregnant” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Spring was the season for war, after the winter rains and before the harvest. The first line sets up the contrast: at the time when kings go out to war, this king stays home. The Ammonite war of chapter 10 goes on without him, as Joab besieges Rabbah, east of the Jordan.

Palace roofs were flat, used for walking and sleeping in the cool of the evening, and from the palace on Jerusalem's ridge David could see down into lower courtyards. Bathsheba was most likely bathing at evening in her own courtyard.

The narrator gives her name, her father and her husband. Uriah is one of David's own soldiers, named among his elite warriors, the Thirty (23:39), and he is away at the war. Her father Eliam is probably the Eliam son of Ahithophel in the same list (23:34), which would make her the granddaughter of David's adviser Ahithophel, who will later join Absalom's revolt. The link is often suggested, but the text never spells it out.

The note that she had just purified herself refers to the washing after her monthly period that the law required. It tells the reader that she was not already pregnant. The child can only be David's.

The chapter is told with cold economy, and one verb runs through it like a chain: send. David sends Joab to war, sends to ask about the woman, sends messengers to fetch her. The man who stays home controls everything by sending. And the Hebrew behind get her is take her. Samuel had warned Israel that a king would take (1 Samuel 8:11-17).
passages.later: Matthew's family tree of Jesus remembers her by this story: ‘David was the father of Solomon by Uriah’s wife’ (Matthew 1:6). And Psalm 51 carries a heading that sets it ‘When Nathan the prophet came to him after his adultery with Bathsheba’ (Psalm 51:1).
passages.hard:
Was Bathsheba a willing partner, or a victim of the king's power?

Readers have disagreed. Some have seen her as sharing the blame, bathing where the king might see and making no protest. Many modern interpreters, among them a growing number of evangelical and Jewish commentators, argue that the text places all the responsibility on David.

Look at what the text says. David sees, sends, takes and lies with her. Every verb of action is his. She is given no speech except the news that she is pregnant. A woman summoned by the king's messengers had little power to refuse. The narrator is careful in the details: she was bathing at evening in what was likely her own courtyard. Nathan's parable in the next chapter casts her as a lamb taken from a poor man, not as a partner in the wrong, and God's judgment falls on David.

The text does not tell what Bathsheba felt. It plainly holds the king accountable for what he did with his power. Nothing in the story blames her.

If you have been harmed by someone with power over you, hear this too. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. The Bible did not blame Bathsheba, and it does not blame you. Please tell someone you trust. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The chapter begins with a king at home when he should have been with his army. Ask what openings idleness and unchecked power give to wrong in your own life. And ask who would pay if you used the power you have to take what you wanted.

passages.happening:
David sends orders to Joab: “Send me Uriah the Hittite” (verse 6). When Uriah comes, David asks how Joab, the troops and the war are doing. Then he tells him, “Go down to your house and wash your feet” (verse 8), and a gift from the king follows him.

But Uriah sleeps at the door of the palace with the king's servants. He does not go home. David asks him why, and Uriah answers, “The ark and Israel and Judah are dwelling in tents, and my master Joab and his soldiers are camped in the open field. How can I go to my house to eat and drink and sleep with my wife? As surely as you live, and as your soul lives, I will not do such a thing!” (verse 11).

David keeps him one more day. He invites Uriah to eat and drink with him and gets him drunk. ‘And in the evening Uriah went out to lie down on his cot with his master’s servants, but he did not go home’ (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
David's plan is plain to the reader. If Uriah goes home to his wife, the child can pass as his. The gift from the king's table is meant to send him home happy.

Uriah refuses, and his reason shames the king. Israel's soldiers on campaign kept away from their wives, and the ark itself was with the army. Uriah is a Hittite by family, a foreigner, and he is more loyal to Israel's army and to its God than Israel's king. Drunk, he is more upright than David sober.

His name is usually taken to mean that the LORD is his light. The great Hittite empire had fallen centuries before, but the Bible uses the name for peoples living in Canaan and for groups linked to later states in Syria. Whatever his ancestry, Uriah is one of David's mighty men.

Notice how sin grows in this chapter. Idleness, a look, a taking, and then a lie. Each attempt to hide the first wrong needs a worse one, and the next one will be a death.
passages.later: The law told Israel's soldiers how to keep their camp: ‘When you are encamped against your enemies, then you shall keep yourself from every wicked thing’ (Deuteronomy 23:9). Uriah keeps it. The king does not.
passages.asks: Uriah would not take a comfort his comrades could not have. Ask whose loyalty around you puts your own to shame. And ask what you are trying to cover that will only need a bigger cover next time.

passages.t: The letter, and the LORD's verdict
passages.happening:
‘The next morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it with Uriah’ (verse 14). In the letter he wrote, “Put Uriah at the front of the fiercest battle; then withdraw from him, so that he may be struck down and killed” (verse 15).

Joab puts Uriah where he knows the strongest enemy soldiers are. The men of the city come out to fight, ‘some of David’s servants fell, and Uriah the Hittite also died’ (verse 17).

Joab sends a messenger with the news, and tells him what to say if the king is angry that the army went so close to the wall: ‘Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead as well’ (verse 21). The messenger reports the losses and ends with those words. David sends back a message for Joab: ‘Do not let this matter upset you, for the sword devours one as well as another’ (verse 25).

‘When Uriah’s wife heard that her husband was dead, she mourned for him’ (verse 26). When the mourning is over, David has her brought to his house, and she becomes his wife and bears him a son. ‘But the thing that David had done was evil in the sight of the LORD’ (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
David sends the letter by Uriah's own hand. The loyal soldier carries his own death sentence back to the front.

Joab understands exactly what the king wants, and he arranges it. Others die with Uriah. The plan to kill one man costs the lives of several of David's soldiers. Joab expects the king to be angry at the losses and to ask why the army went so near the wall. He even imagines David recalling Abimelech, the son of Gideon, killed when a woman dropped a millstone on him from the wall at Thebez. Jerubbesheth is another form of Gideon's name, Jerubbaal. But Joab knows the one sentence that will calm the king.

David's reply is chilling in its coolness. Word for word, he tells Joab not to let this thing be evil in his eyes. The narrator answers with the same word: the thing David had done was evil in the eyes of the LORD. It is the first time God is mentioned in the whole chapter. No human court could reach the king, and the story is told so that he seems to have escaped. The last sentence refuses to let that stand.

Bathsheba mourned for her husband. The text records her grief, and then her marriage to the man who had him killed. It does not say what she felt about either.
passages.later:
Joab's memory goes back to the book of Judges: ‘But a woman dropped an upper millstone on Abimelech’s head’ (Judges 9:53).

Much later, the book of Kings sums up David's life in a single sentence with a single exception: he did what was right all his days, ‘except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite’ (1 Kings 15:5).
passages.hard:
Why does the Bible tell its greatest king's worst sin in such detail?

Because it will not make its heroes exceptions. The story moves slowly, step by step, from idleness to a look, a taking, a lie and a murder, and every attempt to hide the first wrong needs a worse one. The king who was called to do justice and righteousness for all his people (8:15) uses his power to take another man's wife and then his life.

The narrator rarely comments in these books, and he holds back his judgment until the last line. That single sentence carries more weight for having been withheld. Later Scripture keeps the memory: Kings names this one exception to David's faithfulness, and Matthew keeps Uriah's name in the line of Jesus. The honesty is part of the message. No one stands above God's word, not even the king God chose and loved.
passages.asks: David told Joab not to let the matter trouble him, and he thought it was finished. Ask what wrong you have told yourself is finished. And ask whether it is finished in the sight of the LORD.
